newsitem.title: USA: Argentine global bond offer sparks supply worries.
newsitem.headline: Argentine global bond offer sparks supply worries.

text.p: Argentina's announcement it would issue $3 billion bonds in the first quarter won applause on Tuesday from U.S. investors as a bold and swift move by the nation to meet its funding needs.
But investors also expressed concern at the volatility the jumbo deal brings to the market.

"Argentina is building a yield curve and distributing the financial liabilities over a broad spectrum," said Dan Peirce, emerging market debt strategist at Bank of Boston. "It's getting a good chunk of its funding needs out of the way."
The primary risk for U.S. investors are yields of U.S. Treasuries, which could overwhelm the spread risk, he said.

The official announcement of Argentina's bonds issue late Tuesday contained no surprise for U.S. investors who had correctly anticipated the offering of $2 billion fixed rate five year and 20-year bonds.
Economic Minister Roque Fernandez said another $1 billion in other bonds will be issued before March 30.
Argentina needs to raise about $8.0 on the international capital market this year and it had already raised $1.8 billion in December 1996 for 1997 needs.
The volatilities in the U.S. Treasuries in recent sessions may be caused by hedge selling in advance of large dollar-denominatend issues by emerging nations, Peirce said.
Mexico's offering of $1 billion 10-year note announced last Friday is expected to be priced Wednesday.

The trend towards larger size and longer-maturity is beneficial for issuers in terms of economy, but the supply could strain the market, said a fund manager, who blamed the competitive pressure among underwriters to outbid their rivals to get the mandate.
"Underwriters push the envelop until they break it," he said. "The market is finite."
Back in 1994 and 1992, too much paper in the market caused spreads to widen and investors shied away from new issues until the market came back to equilibrium, he said.
"The occurence comes every several years," he said.
With a "sizable" new issuance calendar for emerging market corporate debt in the first quarter, in addition to the sovereign debts, the risk of oversupply is clearly rising, the manager warned.
